title: Heh
hook: the breath sound, added to Abram and Sarai to make Abraham and Sarah

segments.voice: Yesterday, a letter that sounds like a door and sits beside the word for poor. Your line was dalet is a door. Whose door did you open? Today, the letter that's almost nothing but air. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-three.

"Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham." That's God speaking in Genesis, to a man who is already old and has been Abram his whole life. Further on in the same chapter it happens again, to his wife: no more Sarai, from now on Sarah. Two new names, in a single conversation. In English it looks like a few letters shuffled. In Hebrew the change is smaller, and stranger. Each name ends up with the same new letter. And that letter barely makes a sound. It's the letter you'd use to write a sigh.
screen: `ABRAM BECOMES ABRAHAM.` → `SARAI BECOMES SARAH.` → `ONE LETTER, NEARLY SILENT.`

segments.voice: Heh. Start with your own mouth. First, the sound. Say it with your hand in front of your mouth. Heh. No tongue, no lips, no teeth. Just warm air. This sound is about as close as speech comes to simply breathing out. Second, Abram. In Hebrew his name gains a heh in the middle, and becomes Avraham. The verse gives the reason in the same breath: "for the father of a multitude of nations have I made thee." A promise, sealed by adding a breath. Third, Sarai. Her change works differently. The yud at the end of Sarai comes off, and a heh takes its place: Sarah. "As for Sarai thy wife, thou shalt not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall her name be." So both of them, husband and wife, carry the same new letter out of that conversation. Readers have asked why heh, of all letters. Some answer that it's the letter of breath, and a new name is like a new breath of life. Some rabbis go further. In the Talmud, in tractate Menachot, they take a word from Genesis about the heavens and the earth being created, and split it in two: be-heh, with heh, and bera'am, he created them. Their reading: this world was made with this letter, the breath letter. Fourth, what it means for a person. Abraham and Sarah didn't get new faces or new families that day. They got one breath added to who they already were. Some changes are like that. Not a new person. The same person, with a little more air in them.
screen: `THE SOUND OF BREATHING OUT.` · `AVRAHAM: A HEH IN THE MIDDLE.` · `SARAH: YUD OFF, HEH ON.` · `A WORLD MADE WITH HEH.` · then, large: `THE SAME NAME, PLUS A BREATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe out slowly. Settle, and let your shoulders drop. Breathe in through your nose, without forcing it. Then let the air out through an open mouth, long and slow, so it makes the faintest sound: heh. That's the letter. Do it again, and let the breath out be longer than the breath in. If a name comes to mind, yours or someone you love, let it ride on the breath for a moment. If you pray, you can let the breath be a prayer without words. Keep breathing out slowly. The bell holds the time.
Heh. The breath letter, the h sound, added to Abram and set in place of Sarai's last letter. Today's word.
Your line: heh is breath. Today, before you say someone's name, take one slow breath out first, and then say it like it matters. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Children learning the alef-bet may be taught heh by its soft h sound; the renaming of Abram and Sarai in Genesis 17 is read in synagogue as part of the cycle of Torah readings, and some teachers point out the added heh.

original.note: Hebrew: the letter heh, the h sound; also written הֵה.

trapdoor: what you thought: Abram became Abraham with a few extra letters.
what it means: in Hebrew both Abram and Sarai receive the same letter, heh, the breath sound.
what a scholar hears: Menachot 29b reads 'when they were created' in Genesis 2:4 as 'with heh He created them': this world made with the breath letter.
